Would like to thank the developers for this game. I am 67 and been looking for a fps type of game. This game is great. The adventurer setting is ideal pace for me as my fingers are not as nimble anymore. I enjoy the game play, story line and especially the look of the game. Releasing paid DLC instead of fixing pre-existing bugs and issues.

Would I recommend? Yes, but also no depending on what you're expecting from the game.

Why yes?
- Boston Dynamics exits in the 80's and has gone too far, and you're a rude crude teen with attitude and guns
- Guns feel and sound great
- Robot designs are pretty sweet and their sound design is honestly scary at times
- Huge map that feels like it was lived in (for the most part)
- Co-op makes the game amazing, but it can still be fun solo

Why no, depending on what you're expecting?
- Stealth can be a mixed bag. I mean yeah, you can excuse being detected immediately by just saying "You were sprinting everywhere and they're robots, of COURSE they're gonna detect you" But it can be a drag at times
- Nearly all of the houses have either the same or similar layouts. That can make sense given that this game was kind of a side project for Avalanche and it can speed up dev time and bug testing if you have modular assets that can be quickly made to create multiple, slightly different houses. Still can be a bummer at times though
- The weapon pack DLC's, at the time of writing this, can seem kinda pointless. I mean yeah, you'll get mid-tier versions of the weapons from those packs at the point of purchase so you can start a new game with pretty good gear, but the only weapons that seem worth it at the moment are the AS-VAL and RPG from the Soviet pack

What's there to be mixed about?
- As stated before, the stealth can be hit or miss. Sprint everywhere? Gonna get detected fast and chased down for a mile or so. Crawl everywhere? Most likely never gonna be detected but it's gonna take ages to get anywhere. Just gotta be super careful with how you move
- Many players state that they're running out of ammo super fast. That can be remedied three ways. One is to not fight literally every bot you come across, but that means less experience and potential loot however. The second is a skill perk that increases the amount of ammo you loot from any source, up to double the base amount. The third is to find schematics to make your own. I personally have the opposite issue where my storage is being primarily taken up by ammo and I'm always scrapping it to make space, but I can see where other players are coming from
- The player base building is kinda cool at first, but leaves a lot to be desired. Still though, custom base I guess
- Player level cap is 31, leaving you to specialize in your skills pretty hard or be a kinda crumby Jack-of-all-trades. Makes sense in co-op, but kinda sucks in solo
- "Rivals", the mini-bosses of the game, only seem worth fighting once you hit level 25, when they finally have a chance to drop the best weapons in the game. Not saying never fight them until that point, but doesn't seem 100% worth it till you're 25
- Clothing is all pretty cool and reminds me of my childhood, and can give you minor buffs. But the minor buffs may not seem worth it. Like oh cool this jacket gives me 3% bullet resistance and these shoes give me 2% noise reduction. Does it make a difference? I can't tell. But the placebo effect may be kicking in for me I'm not sure.

All in all, this is still a really fun game. Just do yourself a favor and don't jump in expecting Far Cry or GR: Breakpoint style stealth. You don't have to fight absolutely everything, but that's not to say you can't. The best way I can describe this game is S.T.A.L.K.E.R but swap mutants and anomalies out for big AF robots. If possible, pick it up while it's on sale with some friends and roleplay Red Dawn meets Terminator.

Very lukewarm "recommend".

The game has a decent opening and a very interesting setting / scenario. Early on, there is a story to follow.

...however, past the first few hours (out of the tutorial area) the story just kind of stops. it's open world, meaning you're doing the same things over and over again. The quests are simple: go into yet another bunker (all typically smaller than the one in the opening section), turn on the power, get main missions. the main missions are just going to X location, killing more enemies you've already been killing hundreds of, for the reward of a text blurb or a brief, not exactly revealing voiced message. A lot of houses etc. are copypasted, with there being a lack of story or NPC's each location just ends up " a place to loot", and most loot is randomly generated and becomes completely forgettable. 

Side activities like base attack / defense are just plain unfun and barely functional; the attacks involve infinitely, fast respawning hordes of enemies while you're supposed to try and actually break the base and you get zero cover.

Essentially, there's story content for a 5-10 hour game but i played 36 hours and didn't get to the end, i just got finally got bored and opted to stop playing. The game has a lot potential that's untapped, the developers apparently preferred to just make new (stronger) weapons to sell as pricy DLC.

That said... i paid very little for in deep steam sale and the first few hours were really good. As such, if you can get it cheap, play it for a bit but don't bother deep diving into the open world / long term game because there's really just not much there.

Developer has formally stated there will be no further patches or bugfixing, including repairs to the gameplay that were broken by their last major "update". This leaves substantial portions of both the base game and DLCs both unusable or worse than prior to the last update. Paying extra for DLCs that just break your game more frequently is a poor choice; buy base game only, and only at steep discount, and only if you don't mind jank and broken mission chains.

Would not trust this developer again.

This is a tough one to review. It's kind of fundamentally unsatisfying, but it takes you so long to notice that it's at least worth trying out for a few weekends. So is it good? It is, until it isn't...

The atmosphere of being alone & isolated against an overwhelming force trying to genocide you is absolutely top-notch in the early stages, until you eventually get so kitted out that you're just blasting everything for fun. The audio logs and snippets of narrative that you run across are compelling, until you eventually discover that the plot isn't really leading anywhere because absolutely Zero resources were allocated to the narrative other than a few audio logs and notes. The very specific Open World Swedish Countryside is unique to gaming (i think?) and works fabulously, i mean at one point i was just stopped in my tracks as a wind came through the trees and a bunch of fall-colored leaves soared over me in the air... but eventually the dearth of unique game assets starts to pick away at your suspension of disbelief as you loot the same two medkits from the same bathroom in the same house for the 57000th time. The enemy design is great and terrifying and the first time you take down a Tank feels like such a huge deal... and then eventually the 20th time you take one down it's just busywork to try and clear out an area to summon the Optional SuperBoss. Which is fun for all of five seconds, until you realize it's just a bullet-sponge reskin of existing enemies, with unavoidable  insta-kill attacks, and then killing it rewards you with a Slightly Better Rocket Launcher-- the only possible utility of which would have been to use on the boss you have to kill to obtain it. Plus the rocket launcher in this game sucks anyway. It seems like it will be awesome and is fun at first but then you realize it does pitiful damage for something that looks so cool, because it's not balanced very well, nor are any of the weapons or upgrades or stats, because they appear in a game where the (presumably limited) budget went to Style. A game that's so visceral that it hides its fundamental flaws for as long as possible... until it doesn't. 

It's a bad game that takes you 60 hours to notice it's bad, probably because it was made by a fifth of the staff you'd need to execute this concept fully, so is it a bad game? Is a Bad Game one that makes you think you're gradually working towards something when you're ultimately just working towards another few lines of text in yet another cookie-cutter building after fighting yet another battalion of robots that have become as scary as koopas in Mario? I would say that a good game is always good, rather than Only Good At First, and this game is often absolutely fantastic at first... until it isn't. And you only have so much time and money and there is *so* much competition. 

I am pleased to live in a world where Swedish Robot Apocalypse Games exist, as that premise speaks to me, and i do not for a second regret buying Generation Zero, but as for you: only play this if you are invested enough in the very specific idea of Swedish Robot Apocalypses to forgive how GNDN this game is (goes nowhere, does nothing...).

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Setting & Writing[/h3]
Generation Zero has one of the most extensive, realistic and impressive open-world settings you could hope to see anywhere. Miles and miles of countryside, and the occasional larger town, are dotted with the signs of destruction, but still maintain a natural beauty that feels eerie. It’s an impressive duality to have intense firefights in such an idyllic setting, a contrast that enhances both factors. The level of detail is remarkable, with each location having handcrafted parts that make it unique, and a good amount of Easter eggs, secrets and references untied to quests, there just for the sake of exploring.

The writing of the overall lore files, dialogues and story is passable but nothing exceptional. If anything, it makes up for it in sheer volume, and you’ll be able to understand several implied plots and schemes if you pay attention to all the hundreds of recordings and writings found all over. It’s interesting enough (at times), even if not great.

[h3]Exploration & Quests[/h3]
The world is massive and dotted with named points of interest, towns, bunkers and more. Between them you’ll discover Safe Houses, fast-travel hotspots that have a generous (but limited, and upgradeable) stash and various crafting benches, other than vehicle stations to spawn motorbikes and bicycles (they’re crap). There are tons of containers, lockers, bags, cars to loot and scavenge for ammo, crafting materials and loot - you’ll have to open thousands of containers to accumulate enough resources to survive. 

In many locations you’ll find side quests that will mostly task you with finding specific items, destroying a specific enemy, or racing a destination - they’re worthwhile as they represent the bulk of XP gain, but are rather monotonous in their objectives in the long run. Most are marked on your map, although some are obscure and I’ll admit we googled a few because we got stumped.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2949336701

[h3]Combat System[/h3]
The machines are relentless, programmed and built to kill, and you’re just a human. The superiority of your enemy in both numbers and ability is apparent from the start and this constant won’t change until much, much later. A few bullets are all that’s needed to take you down, and unless you get an adrenaline shot (rare / expensive if you have the recipe) you’ll have to respawn at a safehouse. Use cover, study each enemy type’s attack patterns and use consumables like flares, smoke grenades and fireworks to confuse the machines and gain valuable time for your attacks. 

Sometimes, fights draw neighboring machines which in turn alert even more, true mountains of spam that are better retreat from, and try again when things are quieter. Each enemy has unique weak spots you can exploit to permanently damage them, disabling weapons and components through precise and sustained shots. This mechanic is paramount to inflict enough damage to otherwise massive HP sponges. Later on, you may even draw machines of different factions to fight each other and just reap the loot.

[h3]Character Progression & Weapon Customization[/h3]
You’ll gain levels once enough XP is gathered, awarding one perk point to spend in one of the various specializations, with an “ultimate” perk at the end of each. Some focus on combat, others on utility like lockpicking or looting more ammo. Most of them are useless, and that only the combat and tech ones are worth a damn. Weapons have six rarity tiers, becoming better as you loot distant regions and kill more powerful foes, and can be customized with accessories like sights, compensators and more, also tiered in rarity.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2949336588

[h3]Crafting & Base Building[/h3]
You'll be able to craft ammunition, consumables and utility items like a mobile respawn, if you have enough points to unlock the recipes. Points are accumulated by crafting lower-tier items and unlocking better ones, kinda like when you craft 500 iron daggers in Skyrim to grind blacksmithing. These diverse ammon types are better against armor, or may have special effects like fire, electricity, etc. but the latter can be very expensive and require rare resources. The economy in this regard is screwed, with some basic resources like Textiles (to make medkits you need to LIVE) being very scarce, while you’ll never have to worry about ammo ones.

Okay, don't get me wrong...this game DOES have issues... Terrain has actual cracks in it, scenery floating above the ground in many places, you can't quite walk up steps right, the inventory is wonky and items don't stack like they should, and this list could go on for a while. But despite all the negatives, I still enjoy the game.

Many people are saying the same things, "it's boring", "it's too easy", "there aren't enough robots", "there's no point in looting because it's all just the same stuff"

I can agree that there are parts where there isn't any action...so I could see where it could be boring for someone who is used to Call of Duty or something, where you are constantly running and gunning, but this game isn't like that. You wouldn't buy Life and then b*tch because it isn't more like Monopoly, would you? Same idea...it's an FPS...but it's also a sandbox-exploration RPG...

As for being too easy, yeah...at first it is. You come across 1-2 Runners at a time, sometimes there may be 3-4...and they are armed with .32 caliber weapons and have to stand still to shoot you...with their giant "weak point" conveniently sitting, unarmored, on their back for you to easily shoot. Later in the game, those very same Runners are armed with 12 gauge shotguns and full auto 7.62mm machine guns, with turrets that can rotate a full 360 degrees and fire while they are sprinting around...combine that with the fact that you are fighting 15-20 of them at the same time AND there are Seekers, who send out a sonar pulse to pinpoint your location and relay it to all of the surrounding machines, there's a swarm of Ticks that are jumping around attacking you like a f*cking facehugger from the Alien franchise, and then you hear a loud screaming sound behind you...and turn around just in time to be melee attacked with a giant bladed arm of a Hunter... You stand up, dealing with the ridiculously long recovery cutscene, and try to run and apply some first aid...but oh no, there are now 4 more Hunters closing in on you and they are sending a barrage of bullets at you with their .50cal machine guns and one of them is lobbing gas grenades in your direction...

I say, if you think this game is "easy" or there aren't enough robots to fight...you simply didn't play it long enough... I've literally played it for 17 hours and the amount of machines that we encounter has dramatically increased, they are armored, the AI seems more intelligent, and their weapons and sensor systems are becoming more advanced...and we aren't even through the "intro missions" or even stepped foot off of the island that you spawn on...

As far as the looting, yeah, I agree it can be monotonous searching every single house and vehicle, the countless backpacks just mindlessly strewn about, only to find 4 stacks of flares and ammo that you can't even use because you don't have a gun that shoots it... You want to hold on to EVERY piece of loot because other games have conditioned you to "loot all" and keep every scrap because you can vendor it, dismantle it, or use it in a pinch for a big save...but this game isn't like that. You don't need to keep any items that you don't plan on using in the short term...your 2 main weapons, a side arm, first aid kits, the little adrenaline shots, and a stack of ammo that you can load ON your weapon so it doesn't take up space in the inventory...maybe some flares and a gas canister...but almost everything else, either don't loot it, replace existing items, or drop the extras...because nothing is worse than getting to the bottom of a bunker and hearing your buddy find a bazooka and shells, and you have to sit there and manage your inventory because you are carrying around 17 boomboxes and a thousand rounds of ammo for weapons you don't have...

Anyway, I'm very much in love with the game. For every negative against it, there is some positive that balances it, and most of the negatives become trivial because you are too busy saving Sweden from an army of killer robots who are blowing up the entire area with napalm missiles. 

Avalanche is pretty good about listening to the community, and this game literally just came out...give them some time to correct some of the big issues (like item stacking, and some of the UI problems)...and this game could be amazing. At worst case, pick it up on sale, because it's not worth skipping just because the Fortnite generation says that it's too boring...

If I could give any game a "meh" rating, it'd be Generation Zero.

The Good:
+ Combat is amazing in my opinion. Running around, getting the flank on weak spots, and exchanging fire with mech walkers alongside 3 friends is honestly much more fun than I thought it'd be.
+ The sound is great and adds appropriately to the atmosphere of the game. From the gunfire, to the mech noises, to the music, this game does a decent job of setting a tone.
+ The visuals are fantastic. Robot movement is surprisingly smooth (at least for our experience), and the scenery has been created just right. Gorgeous backdrops and coastal villages are done with a level of grandeur I haven't really witnessed in many other games of this genre.

The "meh:"
 -/+ The atmosphere is cool once you're dropped in. You feel enamored with the environment, the emptiness of everything, and the murder-death machines roaming around. The issue comes when you've played for more than a few hours. Everything begins to feel copy/pasted. Much of the scenery quickly loses its artistic touch as you realize it looks like this practically everywhere on a REALLY REALLY big map.
-/+ Enemies are nice to encounter until, once again, you start to piece together that the same 4-5 types of robots you fought within the first 30 minutes become just upgraded/re-colored iterations of themselves throughout the rest of the game. I'm very pleased with design of the enemies on every level, and consider that a plus. And I understand that the devs might be going for quality of enemy designs over quantity, but the disinterest in fighting the same-looking enemies 30 hours into a "story" becomes exponential in its decline. Enemies can also feel extremely bullet-spongy from start to finish. I can see where some like this concept, but it just doesn't do it for me. Situation: I'm facing 8-10 robots (dogs, hunters, etc) with my friends when we all start running out of ammo after only a few kills; soon we're finding ourselves running under fire into fields to loot ammo from robots that POTENTIALLY matches our own. This can be, and has been, neat to see/experience; but ultimately I don't like panicking over ammo or retreating from a fight with 2/3 of the enemies pursuing me because 2-3 of them were extremely bullet resistant.
-/+ Travelling is both enjoyable to a certain extent and a painful walking simulator to another. On one hand, experiencing the environment and atmosphere, whether on a bicycle or on foot, is captivating on some levels. I thoroughly enjoyed the first few hours of running around, getting lost, and eventually ending up where I needed to be. The problem is that Generation Zero essentially forces the player(s) to run across vast amounts of terrain in order to "progress" to the next area before being able to fast-travel. Many games do this, and I don't complain about it normally. Generation Zero is just massive in its landscape and scope of field. In my opinion, it asks too much of the players to run for miles at a time in order to get to the next cookie-cutter objective (more on this in "The Bad" section).

The Bad:
- I'll put this out in the forefront (along with most of the other reviews for this game), but the content is extremely lackluster when it comes down to the final straw. The quote "wide as an ocean, shallow as a puddle" can be aptly applied to Generation Zero. When first starting, it appears there is a lot to offer. A glance at the vastness of the map can build hype, thinking that there's all of this territory to be discovered. That will quickly die after completing a few of the first missions. Once you've cleared 3-4 bunkers and received the same "oh. we've moved...again...come find us at <insert coordinates here>" you start to paint the picture that this game is sending you on a wild goose chase. And unfortunately, you'd be right. You never catch up to any humans that can communicate an exposition to you, and are instead tasked with collecting notes and audio logs that barely explain how things ended up the way they did. This makes any concept of a "story" almost non-existent, and makes the player chase after phantoms to find information.
- The guns seem very weird to me. Don't get me wrong: gunplay and firefights in Generation Zero are what make this game enjoyable. The guns themselves just seem rare in diversity and you don't really tell a difference when using different firearms in an engagement. With a bunch of friends, you can expect to waste the same amount of ammo with a pistol as you would with a rifle, making the guns kind of just this thing in your hands to do a job. From my experience with the game, this meant that guns became more of a preference of what you wanted to shoot versus what could be practical in an approach.
- Scaling is done horrendously in my opinion (on two different levels). I started a solo game and ended up dominating most of the initial enemies. The moment I had any of my buddies join, the difficulty and damage of the mechs sky-rocketed. Suddenly we found ourselves running out of ammo at the onset of engagements and dying rather quickly to enemies that I had otherwise experienced no trouble downing while playing solo. The second tier to this complaint is how the enemies begin scaling after a crossing to the mainland. From that point on, the robots soaked up rounds from even our best kit'd firearms with ease. More often than not, we found ourselves all dying rather quickly and getting stuck while attempting to progress to that next empty bunker with scraps for story exposition.
- Inventory management goes hand-in-hand with the scaling and combat from my standpoint. One of my friends left a negative review based primarily on how the inventory is managed, and I would have to agree with him. We discovered that we had to empty all of our pockets just to carry enough ammo to hope to make it to the next zone. This meant that picking up new items/guns forced us to sacrifice combat potential (aka bullets/older weapons) and hope that we didn't encounter something along the way.

Conclusion:
All in all, I feel this game actually has a lot to offer, and I had many thrilling moments with my friends. I just feel that a definitive amount of content needs to be added and reduce some of the scaling. Overall, I cannot recommend the game at this juncture. A decent game with good concepts, Generation Zero just needs some more time in the oven.

-----------------------------------------------Back Up instructions--------------------------------
For those who are looking on how to create a simple Backup for Gen Z, Go to Documents, search for "Avalanche Studios. Double click on the Avalanche Studios file. Once you have done that you will see the Generation Zero Folder, Right Click on your mouse and copy it. After you have copied it, I Recommend you create an alternate folder to place the Backup Save in. It is Recommended to name it so you are able to easily find it in case something happens to your active save.


If a Corruption within the Auto Save system happens, head back to your Backup Generation Zero folder via documents, which you have created, copy the Backup Generation Zero file and go to the Avalanche Studios file. Once you are on the Avalanche Studio file, Double Click again and you will see the Generation Zero file. That is the one you need to replace with your Backup Save. Simply paste the Backup file that you have copied before and paste it, you will see a message saying "This Destination has (Number) of Files with the same Name." All you have to do once this appears is press "Replace the Files in the Destination." Once you have done that reload the game and the Save should load all your stuff prior to the Corruption.

The biggest issue with the game is the scavenging. The game requires that the player spend time looking for weapons and ammunition, as should be expected. However, the issue with this is that ammo can be rather difficult to come by. This is for two reasons. One is that the loot sources in the world, meaning ammo boxes, backpacks, etc, are not a lucrative source of ammo. In addition, between the many sizes of ammunition, as well as the variants of those sizes, it is often impossible to find ammunition for the weapon that the player wishes to use. The second reason that ammunition is rare is that the best source of ammo is the machines. A player will fire far more rounds than the machine will give, and there is no promise that the ammo found is the one the player wants. Further, the machines themselves are problematic, which leads me to my next point.

The machines are, to put it simply, bullet sponges. They are over-armored with tiny weak points that are near impossible to hit for a variety of reasons, such as the poor sensitivity settings, the poor bullet spread while hip firing, and the speed at which the machines move. On top of that, anything larger than the dog machine has multiple weak points that must be hit for the most ammo effective kill. This is in addition to the fact that the larger machines will require the player to constantly move behind the machine to see half of the weak points, meaning that the player will have to get dangerously close to engage the enemy properly. This leads to the next point, which is the combat.

The combat is not fun, nor is it strategic. The most effective way to engage any larger machine is to run around it in a circle. This is negated by the fact that the player will likely, if not always, be engaging multiple machines at a time. This ranges from fighting about 5 machines, to fighting as many as 20 depending on aspects such as the initial size of the group, whether or not the machines can spawn more machines (which half of them can), and the surrounding terrain (as the player might inadvertently activate enemies in another area while fleeing). Further, range becomes an obnoxious issue to work around. Long range engagements are nearly impossible, as the machines will spot the player as soon as they open fire. Close range engagements are not possible, as the machines will often be too grouped up, or will utilize melee, flames, gas etc. to push the player back.

The machines' styles of engagement are also bad. Large groups of smaller machines will get as close to the player as possible, making them a fast moving in-your-face target that is more of a hassle than an actual obstacle. This is because they will likely be supplemented by the medium and large machines, which will fire missiles, explosives, gas, snipers etc. to keep the player moving. This means that the player will be constantly running from/eliminating smaller enemies, whilst simultaneously trying to ward off larger enemies. The player's attention is never allowed to be focused, and the player is never allowed to remain in one location. This is counter intuitive, as the machines' attacks are the most effective against the player when the player is in the open. Combat becomes moving in a circle from one semi-defensible location to the next, trying to time the attacks of the machines, all while downing dozens of health packs. The machines may be unique and fun to engage when playing with friends or against smaller groups, but alone and/or against larger groups of enemies, combat is a chore.

The snipers are next to useless, not only because of the aforementioned reasons, but also because they are really only useful in very specific circumstances, usually being engagements with smaller enemies. Shotguns are bad, because getting up close to enemies is not a good idea, and slugs are as good as using a sniper. The primary weapons of choice, SMG's and automatic rifles, are the most effective, but as they will see the most use, will burn through ammunition unreasonably fast. Even the rocket launchers take an unfair amount of ammunition to take down large enemies, which are the only worthwhile targets for them. This is in addition to the fact that explosives of any kind seem to do unbalanced damage to weak points, meaning firing rockets will be rolling the dice to see what components actually take damage.

Stealth is another issue. The game's enemies are very aware of the player, so getting close is not an option. Stealth isn't so much sneaking around enemies as it is avoiding them altogether. This is hard to do because of the density of the enemies in any given area, as well as the terrain often limiting traversal options. Stealthily eliminating enemies is not an option, except for smaller enemies with one or two weak points. Any large enemies, however, must be avoided altogether, as firing at them, even at weak points and from great distances, will alert them of your location before they can be destroyed. This will alert all enemies in the area, and turn what was a stealthy operation into a firefight.

Crafting was clearly not thought out. While crafting is extraordinarily useful, it requires two things: schematics and materials. Gathering schematics is either done with a guide, or by painfully moving from location to location and searching every room of every building of every town. Care to guess which most players choose? The materials are very painful to gather, as inventory space is limited, with next to no options to expand it. This means that gathering materials for crafting is essentially carrying around loads of junk in addition to your already heavy necessary equipment. I'd say that most of the time, when I was at my lightest, I had about one third of my inventory open. When scavenging, actually useful materials take up a good portion of that remaining space, which leaves next to nothing for crafting materials.

Equipment rarity. Ugh. As expected, the rarer the equipment, the better it performs. However, the game does not really feature high tier loot areas. Instead, it spawns high level enemies, which will provide the high tier loot. However, the game is not totally clear how powerful any enemy really is, meaning the average player cannot gauge their chances of getting high tier loot from a given enemy. This is also in addition to the fact that the powerful enemies are often larger enemies, which means that they will move with groups of smaller enemies accompanying them.

The UI is terrible. Some other people mentioned it, but the inventory really just does not carry enough, and the UI doesn't give you access to all the stuff you need fast enough. The map is cluttered, sensitivity needs more options, there are too many things to worry about when looting and reorganizing, and the skills.

The skills are garbage. To redo skills, the player needs high tier loot. Great. Then, if you mis-click, miscount your skill points, or just make a mistake, too bad! Get back to grinding!

There's a skill further down the tree that, when maxed out, gives 10% extra damage. When using fully automatic weapons. In single fire mode. Think about that. If you invest heavily into a skill, and then disable yourself from rapid fire capability, you can do 10% extra damage! Wow! It's a rip-off. Just like this game.

I have heard a lot of people discussing this game and talking about how it gets very boring and tedious after 8-10 hours of gameplay. I have played this with some friends for a little over an hour now... and its already hit the boring and tedious part. This game is labeled as a 'post apocalyptic survival horror' by both the developers and the steam tags, so my group of friends and I started it up with that expectation. That went out the window immediately, and I think the games biggest problem is a lack of understanding of what it wants to be.

Does it have survival horror elements? yes. It has your typical level up, buy skills with points system you find in most such games. It has stealth mechanics for sneaking around enemies and looting mechanics as you kill the robots. It does not have a crafting system, which can be good or bad depending on your opinion on the matter. The atmosphere is great with a beautiful world and weather system, the robots look odd and unusual, and their appearance coupled with the atmosphere gives a sense of foreboding dread.

All sounds good right? well...

The intimidation factor of the robots only lasts a few seconds before you realize they are a complete non-threat. in the first five minutes of gameplay, every one of us had a pistol and hundreds of rounds of ammunition each, before we even saw an enemy. We then shortly discovered every enemy in the starting area could be put down by one or two shots of the starting pistol, and drop more ammo than it takes to bring one down. Are you seeing where this is going? Rather than sneaking about and setting ambushes, traps and using tactics, the easiest, safest, and fastest method of dealing with enemies was to simply charge into a group of them and mow them down. Well, there goes the 'horror' claims. Now what about survival? Well, you dont need food, water or sleep. the only loot there is to find is guns, ammo and consumables that make the fights even easier than they already are. This doesnt sound like survival... this sounds like a looter-shooter. I started having flashbacks to Farcry: Blood Dragon, and the 80's music and themes hardly convinced me otherwise. Well, is it at least post apocalyptic? Not by looking at it. Everything looks peaceful and serene; yes you find the occasional house with bloodstains on the wall, but the bloodstains cover a perfectly set up chessboard and checkers set, alluding more to a severe bloody nose than a violent struggle. Cars are abandoned on the road, but seem entirely intact, notes are left everywhere, alluding to stashes and the like, but there's no people, bodies or even signs of life or death. Its a very boring apocalypse by all accounts, and based on how difficult the robots are, it only brings up the mystery of where everyone vanished to, because it sure wasn't the robots chasing them away.

On top of this the game has vast stretches of... nothing. small clusters of easy robots guard small clusters of buildings or houses, and a ten minute run through vast, empty landscape will let you reach the next trivially easy fight where you gather even more ammunition to pack your bags with for the easy fights to come. It feels to me like in the beta there were far more robots to justify the obscene ammunition given to you but that too many people complained about the robot numbers. So instead of patrolling robots, large clusters to fight at key points and enough ammunition to stay alive if you were careful, you end up with vast swathes of emptiness, more ammunition than a man can reasonably carry, and 70% of your playtime just holding shift and W.

The shooting is good, it feels meaty and cathartic and the resulting explosion as a robot dies is satisfying. but its over too soon, and then you're left horrifyingly bored as you sprint to the next beacon in the darkness, which is the next full on firefight. The only time the game becomes truly terrifying and difficult is when the bugs rear their ugly head; party members suddenly being flung into the sky and dying of fall damage for stepping on a twig. Robots evading your shots because they've been consumed by a wall or are jerkily teleporting around you at several thousand miles per hour. The menu does not, for some unknown reason, actually tell you what is in your inventory without clicking on each and every item individually.

I dont recommend this game right now. It feels like its still in beta and has a metric ton of things to be tweaked and sorted out. It looks fun and wonderful if you watch videos of it online, but those are the highlight reels of the 20% of the game spent actually doing something.

Criminally underrated game. Why it hasn't received more attention is baffling to me.

The environment is beautiful. Dense forests that go through seasons. Green in spring, leaves falling in Autumn, and snow in winter. Expansive and open to boot. If you can see it, you can go there. I don't normally, write reviews, but I was looking at the "most helpful" reviews for the last 30 days, and saw that the top two were negative.  Which is fine, people are allowed not to like the game, but I did wonder why they didn't like it.  Upon reading those reviews, I was genuinely left wondering if we were playing the same game.

Before going any further, a caveat.  Neither of these reviewers stated what difficulty level they were playing on.  Possibly, it was one of the higher ones and their take on the gameplay is bang on.  My review should be read strictly in the context of the default difficulty level, which is the level at which I completed my playthrough.

Now,l I don't want to get bogged down in to much TL;DR; detail here.  The core criticism leveled by both of these reviews seems to be that, outside of the starting areas, you get swarmed by enemies that can't be avoided.  I'm, like, *what* are they talking about?

Yes, it's true that the density of enemies, once you leave the starting area, increases significantly.  They are also of progressively higher level, the deeper you get into the map, and the Apocalypse tier mechs really can spot you from a mile away if you don't take care.  If any of these higher-tier mechs spot you, particularly if they are in a pack (which the almost always are), then you will die tired and with brown pants.  But the idea that you cannot sneak past these enemies "without crawling across the map on your belly" is absurd.  To be specific about it:

You absolutely can both run away from and hide from the Azalea/Firebird (the flying ones) mechs.

You absolutely can avoid detection by *any* mech, including Apocalypse Tier, and you can escape even packs once detected.

But not if you play like Rambo.  Running and gunning will get you dead.  I mean, there are probably players that can do that and get away with it, but I am not one of them. 

Anyway, the solution to the quantity/quality threat is simple:

1) 
As soon as possible, maximize all of your stealth attributes. Your early game build should be razor-focused on minimizing your audio and visual signature.  Do that and, so long as it is nighttime, you can ride past FINX-Tier mech while riding a bicycle at a distance of 50 yards and it will not notice you (so long as it is in patrol mode and not actively searching).   Note, however, that these higher-tier mechs frequently deploy picket mechs around their perimeter, and those will spot you if they switch to active scanning.  Apocalypse-Tier mechs require more respect; you will need to stay in cover and duck-walk to avoid detection. 

By the same token, manufacture Apparel that enhances Silence and Camouflage.   Between Skills and Apparel, you can easily get your visibility reduced by 50%, which is enough to let an Apocalypse-Tier Hunter *literally* walk over you without seeing you (if you are prone and in cover [such as high grass], and it is not in Search Mode).  This will also hide you from Firebirds.

2)
Realize that there are *always* more mechs around than you can see.  Some of the larger mechs can spawn smaller mechs but, beyond that, there are always smaller mechs in the vicinity of the larger ones, and they will com running when the shooting starts.

3) 
If you are playing solo, picking a straight-up fight with any of the larger mechs (hunters and up) in the open is borderline-suicidal.  Avoid contact until you can dictate the terms of the engagement.  Ideally, this will mean you are set up in a large barn, bunker, hangar,  or house before you engage.  Structures in this game are indestructible, but explosions can damage you through walls, poison gas can leak into the structure, and enemies can and will shoot you through broken windows and open doors.

4) 
Learn the audio cues for each mech and what kind of attack (kinetic, explosive, pyrotechnic, gas, melee, Ticks) it advertises, then respond accordingly.  

5) 
Learn the weak points of each mech.  More importantly, learn which armaments of each mech pose the greatest threat and how to disable it.  For instance: shooting the shoulder-mounted weapon off of a Hunter reduces its threat level against a player *under cover* by 95%.  For this reason alone, acquiring the top-tier sniper rifle  (the .50 cal Pansarvärnsgevär 90) is strongly recommended.

6)
For the solo player, the only Specialization that matters is Hacking  The best strategy for dealing with packs is "let's you and him fight".  You get full XP for any kill made by your hacked mech. and it costs you nothing but popcorn. In particular, hacking Firebirds should become automatic (bring extra popcorn; those things are a terror)  You may even find yourself picking off or disarming some enemies in order to extend the life of your proxy (this is safe, because mechs involved in combat with each other will not break off to attack you, even if you are attacking them).  And, frankly, the only sane way to kill a Firebird (flying tank mech.) is to hack it first.  A hacked mech will not attack you, even if you shoot it).

A word of caution, however: mechs *hate* being hacked and, when the hack wears off, the will be *pissed* and they will know where you were when you initiated the hack.  If you don't want them to find you, be somewhere else.


Another consistent criticism seemed to be that all there is never enough ammunition.  This statement baffles me.  I am *drowning* in ammunition with just the stuff I find. The only ammo I ever manufacture is the .50 cal for the P-90.  Everything else I find so much of it that I usually just recycle it.  But, context is important.  I am an inveterate Loot Goblin and will search every structure, shipping container and dead mech and loot *everything* off if it. If this is not your style, then yes, you might have logistical issues in regard to ammo.

To put real numbers on this, my typical ammo loadout is:

1500 rounds each of 7.62 FMJ and AP.
2000 rounds each of 5.56 FMJ and AP. 
200 rounds of .270 Soft Tip
200 rounds of .44 Magnum FMJ
150 rounds of.50 BMG FMJ
60 rounds of .50 BMG AP

Once you have acquired enough ammo to reach these targets, and have enough extra in storage to completely replace that twice, recycle anything else you find.

For firing that ammo, i carry:

Automatgevär 4 - Silenced (7.62)
Kvm 89 SAW w/recoil suppressor (5.56)
Älgstudsare Hunting Rifle - Silenced (.270)
"Pansarvärnsgevär" (Pvg 90) (.50 BMG)
.44 Magnus (sidearm) w/recoil suppressor  (.44 Mangum)

Frankly, I could ditch the .44 Magnus and never miss it.

Use the Automatgevär 4 for dealing with runners and ticks at short and medium ranges
Use the Älgstudsare for sniping Runner fuel tanks at long range without being detected.
Use the Kvm 89 SAW when you get swarmed or surprised, to blast an escape path.
Use the Pvg 90 to disarm/kill Huners and tanks at range (the longer the better).

Be aware that firing the Pvg. 90 will advertise your location to every mech. withing a kilometer of your firing location; they *will* be dropping by to pay their respects. Also note that you will likely never find enough .50 BMG ammo in the field to maintain your supply, so you will have to manufacture it.  Looting all the Steel (or items than can be recycled to obtain Steel), Lead and Explosives you can find is critical to provisioning this weapon.

Beyond the guns and ammo, my standard loadout consists of five grenades, a couple of fireworks (they confuse mech targeing systems; useful for escaping ambushes/pursuit) and every  First Aid Kit I can find (not the Paramedic Packs, though; they are intended for group play and are too heavy for the benefit they provide).

The final general criticism is in regard to the storage mechanic.  As a Loot Goblin, I have to agree: I *hate* limited storage that I have to manage.  As a game design decision, I think it is the correct implementation; being forced to limit the available gear is part of the challenge, regardless of how much my packrat personality hates it.

They really released a final update saying "Hi! thank you guys so much! this is our final update, no more updates to this game, we're working on new stuff! baiii!" in the description, meanwhile they changed all the crafting requirements for first aid kits and adrenaline shots (VERY basic consumables) to need an UNHINGED amount of crafting materials, not to mention weapon augments. You guys just made crafting/upgrading anything take at least 5 hours, and you dont even touch broken things that your community has been yelling about for YEARS at this point. You killed your game for no good reason, Id suggest that nobody purchase a game from these people in the future.

Even high end PC's may only have 250m of draw distance before the machines pop-out, where a good laptop might have 4-500m. It's entirely random and makes 2 challenges unobtainable, and has persisted through the last 4 updates at least with no fix in sight, so do be mindful of this.
Solid 9/10
A WORD OF WARNING
If you value your save data on PC and in the Cloud, Do Not, under any circumstances, play this game on a steam deck. It fails to acquire the cloud save, doesn't warn you about it, launches anyway, and overwrites your save file with the blank one you've just started playing. It's not unique to GZ, there's a myriad of games with the same problem, but this is the first one I've encountered, so I feel it the decent thing to do to warn you, fine traveller of the reviews section.
Take it from someone who had 205 hours or progress stolen from him irrevocably. Make a backup of your save file.

PROS:
+ A vast, beautiful landscape. The environment looks really, really good and includes a day/night cycle along with rain and fog. 
+ Character models are decent and move well. 
+ Lots of clothing to find, so you can look however you want (unless you care about stats, in which case, see the CONS note about clothing).
+ A nice assortment of firearms and different types of ammunition for each. 
+ Lots of additions to your weapons, such as scopes, silencers, magazine extenders, etc. 
+ You're fighting robots. Robots may not be a new idea by any means, but at least you're not mowing down zombies or Nazis or Nazi zombies or whatever else has been done to death.
+ No blood or gore because you're killing robots. Normally I don't mind blood and gore (although some games go way over the top), but the lack of blood and gore means this game is more appealing to those who actively dislike it. 
+ The game auto-saves every time you go someplace new, quit, or enter and leave any menu. Sometimes I force a save by going to my inventory and then going back out. 

NEUTRAL:
+/- Although the game constantly auto-saves, you always appear at a safe house. The developers stated this was done to prevent the player from reappearing in the middle of an area swarmed by machines. For the most part, this works fine, but it's a bit annoying if you were a fair distance away from the closest safe house and you need to quit.  
+/- This game is practically made for co-op. I think that's a good thing because my wife and I play this together, but if you prefer to play solo, then this game will probably feel pretty lonely. As a solo game, there isn't enough to keep most players interested for long. 
+/- No survival game mechanics. Personally, I think this is a good thing. I hate having to spent 99% of my time acquiring food and water simply so I can survive another day to repeat the process. That's not my idea of fun, so I'm glad we don't need to eat, drink, sleep, and that the weather doesn't affect us. That said, some people might not share my view, so I'm adding this here in the NEUTRAL category as more of a "heads up" than a judgement. 

CONS:
- Massive disconnection issues. I'm the host and my wife gets disconnected at least once (usually two or three times) per session.
- Experience bugs, such as my wife earning 100 XP every time she enters an area, even if she's been there before. As the host, I don't earn 100 XP every time I enter an area, but for some reason the game thinks she's never been there before so it acts as if it's new for her.
- Experience isn't shown correctly on the team screen. On the team screen, it appears as if my wife is well over a level ahead of me, but when I look at her skills screen (by physically viewing her monitor) she's only slightly ahead of me. 
- Inconsistencies regarding loot. Sometimes items or weapons will be instanced, so we both get them, but other times it's "whoever picks it up first gets it." There's no discernible reason for this other than buggy code. 
- Some skill trees are worthless, not because they're less useful, but because they're bugged. One such skill line should allow players to hack enemy machines, but it doesn't work. 
- There's no way to respec, so you can easily gimp your character by putting points into a less useful line or a line that you don't particularly like. Worse still, some skill lines are broken, so the points put into that line are wasted. 
- You can't split stacks of items (like ammo, medkits, flares, etc) so you can't "give a few medkits" to a co-op partner. You either give them everything or give them nothing. 
- Enemies can see through walls. Normally this isn't a huge issue because they can't shoot through walls, but it's annoying to see a warning indicating that an enemy sees you when you're in a safe house (especially if it's a bunker). 
- Enemies sometimes respawn in places they shouldn't. One time my wife and I were surprised by enemies appearing out of thin air (and I mean they literally popped in) inside an underground bunker that we'd cleared out that's also a safe house. No enemies should appear there, period. 
- There's a distinct lack of information when it comes to weapons and ammo. Sure, there's a small blurb about what this or that weapon does and how this ammo works, but there are no stats to go with it. It's great to know that AP and FMJ ammo do more than HP, but HOW MUCH more? 
- The world may look nice, but it feels empty and lifeless. This isn't just because the players are the only humans around, but because all the towns and cities feel like props, not houses that were used and lived in. 
- Bikes are terrible. They steer horribly and are only useful on roads, which partially defeats the advantage of a bike over a normal car. 
- Clothing has random stats, which means you could easily find yourself facing that old and worn RPG dilemma: "Do I wear what looks good or do I wear what gives me the most benefit?" If you're interested in the latter, expect to look like a blind hobo. 
- You can't trade clothing. Finding clothing is completely randomized as is what type and color you pick up, so it's frustratingly common to find clothing your co-op partner might want (and vice-versa) with no way to switch them out. 
- No melee weapons. Some enemies can run close to you very quickly, so having a knife or a bat or a sword could be useful. 

VERDICT: Generation Zero is a great idea and overall, it's a fun game to play co-op with people you trust. Unfortunately, there are a lot of bugs and poor design decisions that really hurt it. Honestly, this game feels like an Early Access title because it still needs a lot of work concerning ease-of-use and playability. 

Assuming you can get used to the negatives (or at least ignore them) and you have at least one person to play co-op alongside, I'd still recommend getting it. Just be warned that you might run into more than a few problems, not the least of which are the connectivity issues my wife has been dealing with.

I really wanted to love this game. I am a big fan of "walking sims", which are normally boring for most of people. I enjoy walking through wide open areas, encounter rare enemies with some tactical approach, discover interesting places. I like beautiful graphics and landscapes. 

I pre-purchased this. The concept of fighting robots is really good in my opinion. Fighting human bots can kill the immerse in case of bad AI. And in case of robots it will not feel really detached if they stuck somewhere / dont notice you etc. They are robots. Also robots can be very different which means that will allow to build completely different enemies with different behavior,capabilities etc, which means variety of gameplay. 2. Bunkers. Omg this is a nighmare. No minimap. Every bunker is built based on same assets / textures and looks like randomly generated set of corridors. In every bunker you need to power on generator which you can find only by opening every single door and checking every corner.

I'm not going to praise this game into heaven, because it's not that good. But it is definitely worth a try. I'll begin with the first impressions, then tell something about the general gameplay and finally the replay value. 

First impressions:
When Ifired up the game for the first time I had already read a few reviews, which were mixed. I had read about bug reports, crashes, but also about the massive immersive world and the machines. The latter were enough to make me buy the game. 
The game starts fast and smooth; within 30 seconds I was inside the game world. Nice! 
I found myself on a shore, close to a small house. The looting began. I expected a survival game and was pleasantly surprised I picked up my first gun right at the start. At least some shooting to do!
Finding stuff and managing your inventory was pretty easy, which I like. Not too much struggles with tons of items and crafting stuff, that isn't really my thing. I like looting and action, which I went for right away. My first encounter with machines was delightful.  I found out the shooting mechanics are very good and the enemies look and move realistic. They seem to be pretty clever and you can play with them, knowing there's danger in their behaviour. 
To sum it up, a pretty good first impression. No bugs or crashes (I use Windows 10 and have a descent machine) other than some sheds that are hard to enter because the floors aren't aligned with the surface they're built on. So far so good!

General gameplay:
I already mentioned machine behaviour. They are cool! They are clever, and the variety of machines is awesome. Although there's only 6 types of machines, their appearance and behaviour is so distinctive that you have your hands full. You need to find certain approaches and see what your weapons do to them in order to find what weapons are best suited to take them out. Their hit boxes are well thought out. Aiming for delicate machinery parts and the head pays off. Bigger enemies are very challenging in the beginning, and by making clever use of explodable devices is the way to go with those. 
The game world is fantastic. You really imagine yourself in a living environment. Especially the lighting effects are crazy. As if ray tracing was already applied. Really impressive! Many people complain that there's a lack of variety in buildings and stuff, but I disagree. Of course, not every house is unique, there's a somewhat small stock of basic buildings that are accessible and the inside seems rendered through algorithms, so sometimes you find a house with 3 bathrooms (!) and just two bedrooms, but who cares. The fact that there's a certain repetition in the houses means it will be easier to find loot boxes in them. 
The way the world is filled with differing areas and villages, is very natural and perfectly balanced. And if you know Sweden you will notice it is actually a very good resemblance. 
The quests you pick up and follow throughout the game, scattered like breadcrumbs on the moth obvious path, are nice. You are searching for answers to what the hell happened to the people, and I found it funny enough to do. Sometimes you loose track of a mission because you might have picked up stuff previously before the mission starts. That can be a bit confusing, but the menus help you out with a good overview of all activities. 
The game is designed to be played cooperatively with 4 players max. But you can go hunting alone easily. However, playing with a buddy or two can be joyful. There's a complicated skill tree that obliges you to follow certain specializations, because with ranking up you can't gather enough skill points to get all the skills. That encourages you to find a specialization that will suit best with other players. Like medic skills, or sniper skills, or explosive damage etc. 
It's not always easy to connect to other players. Most fun is to play this game with friends. But you can also find random players. If everything works well, that is. There's occasions where connecting to others causes the game to crash. The way people connect to eachother is actually not very stable. But on many occasions I was able to connect with friends and we had a great time together :)

Replay value:
I have spent close to 200 hours in the game now. I finished my carreer completely and ranked up my first character to the max (level 31). I also started the 3 other characters and was working my way through getting the second char, up to speed. You can have 4 characters max and you can form each of them in your own way, making different choices in the skill tree. This is a clever approach and would definitely add to the replay value. However, there's certain things that don't. 
First of all there's the bug fixing and tweaking the devs do to the game based on player feedback. They handle the game in a way as if it was an early release game. They completely change loot regeneration, item drops and damage for explosives. They even tweak the main missions based on the player feedback. 
Well, at least they take care of flaws and bugs, but they really seem to overdo it. I like a game to be somewhat predictable. I hate it when after a tweak suddenly you won't find certain ammo types anymore, or your explosive devices only do a 3rd of the damage they used to do. Essentually, my opinion is that all these settings were pretty good when the game launched. The tweaking had some good results, on adrenaline shot drops in the game world for example. But on many occasions they broke some coold features instead of making things better. And they always managed to fuck something up elsewhere, needing to patch that the next time, or even hotfix a patch because the game became unplayable for a group of people. Weird.
The devs promise an evolving game world where new areas will be unlocked, more quests will arrive and more enemies and features will be added overtime. This is what I really am hoping for, because after my 200 hours and not enough friends to play the game with I'm done now. I got annoyed by faulty updates, where they messed up the gameplay. Suddenly lots of loot boxes were empty and big enemies would take so many rockets / explosives / bullets to bring them down it was almost unplayable. For each now you had to spend an hour looting before you would have enough to face another big one. And the stuff they would drop wasn't even a fraction of the ammo you'd need to kill them. They have recently fixed that problem (june update 2019) but it scared me away from the game. The fun factor was suddenly gone.

Conclusion: 
I think this game is worth its 35 bucks. It has a great environment, nice story, good coop and excellent gameplay due to clever AI enemies and good shooting mechanics. The light effects are simply brilliant. 
I've had lots of fun with this game and if you are the type of person that can stand a slowly evolving game where you have to spend time to get good gear and find bigger enemies, you're going to have fun too. Most bugs seem fixed now, so hopefully they paved the way for new content. This game definitely has potential. 
Many people complain that the world is too empty. Not enough enemies, not enough things happening around you... well yeah, let's make yet another farcry game where everything is chewed through for you so that every 12 year old can find its path towards big guns and rep. Nah, seriously, I think the game is good. It's full enough in my opinion. It certainly offers excitement and can be thrilling when you suddenly find yourself cought by a patrol of machines, or enter an area with just more enemies than you'd expected. 
Let's hope the devs don't let themselves push too far from their original ideas with the game, because it is good and balanced.  And lets hope for all the new stuff that is being promised. 
The game is advertised to being a survival game, but I wouldn't call it like that. It's more like an open world adventure with lots of shooting :)

Full review
I was very excited for this. It's the first game I've bought day 1 in many years. Is it everything I hoped for? No. Am I upset at it? Also no. It's no genre defining, massive blowout, amazing game. It's slower paced with spurts of action tossed in. I'm not happy that the buildings are all almost exactly the same. and the loot is meh. There's not really a sense of danger most of the time either. I've had several "oooooh s#!t no no no no no!" moments that are amazing but it's mostly walking around (a beautiful setting) and managing your inventory. The "mystery" falls rather flat pretty quick also. Robots showed up, pew pew pew, nobody knows what's going on, wander around and "piece it together". It's bland and doesn't carry the game at all. It seems more like an excuse to have a game and not a reason to play it.

The gameplay itself  is pretty good though. There's plenty of flexibility in how you approach situations. Do you go in b@lls out? Do you skirt around and avoid it completely? Maybe hang back and snipe weak points? Do you lure them in with a flare or radio and blow up a gas tank? Lure them in, disrupt their targeting with fireworks and then blast them? Plenty of options are available and with friends you could really have some fun with it and get pretty tactical. You can lone wolf it and spread out your skills or specialize in a particular area and use teamwork. 

I've seen a lot of people mention bugs and crashes. I have only had the game crash one time and no other bugs. I have had one time in one spot where a robot was shooting at me through a wall but no big deal. I don't know what others are experiencing. Like I said, my rig is pretty good but I'm not doing anything else while playing. I'm not streaming, game capture or anything like that. I'm just playing the game and on discord talking to friends. I will say though that the bandwidth issues need to be addressed immediately. 

As beautiful as the exterior world is, the building interiors are equally as bad. Boring, cookie cutter buildings with identical clutter gets really old really fast. On the one hand, you can speed loot hella fast because of it but in reality, looting buildings quickly becomes tedious due to their bland interiors.

Overall I do still like the game. The map is huge and beautiful and the gameplay doesn't rely on quick twitch, crazy good reflexes in a competitive pew fest. I enjoy it's slow pace, beautiful scenery, amazing audio and interesting concept. But you should really know what you're getting into. You don't get this game for great story, compelling characters or groundbreaking features. You get it to tactically play our own version of Red Dawn against robots. In the end, it's a good game that needs some more polish and tweaking.

My initial impressions of this game were pretty positive. A semi-survival game (that wasn't about zombies), set in the 80's and in rural Sweden. It all seemed pretty fresh, especially when combined using Avalanche's Apex engine which was also interesting. But after around 15 hours the negatives really started to take ahold.

[b]Pros+[/b]
+ Interesting, unique location
+ Exceptional environment, wonderfully rendered world
+ Weather effects (fog, rain, wind, etc)
+ Sound design is excellent
+ It's the 80's! (might be a con to some, lol!)
+ Gunplay is fairly well done

From the moment I spawned in to the first house I looted I was like, wow..... "This game looks great." Environments were well rendered with trees swaying, leaves cascading as the wind was blowing. Sky boxes look great, either when it was night or day. Lighting is well done and indoor environments were just the same; richly populated with possessions that implied, "wow, people really lived here." 

Sound design is excellent, from the echo of gunshots in the distance, to concussive blasts, machine movement and actions, to the simplicity of the lake water calmly rolling on the shore was all hard not to be immersed by.     

The Gunplay also is quite well done. Weapons all have satisfying animations and sound effects, with pleasing impacts on the machines as they spark, ricochet and dismantle armor and other components as it registers the damage

[b]Cons-[/b]
- Bugs (lots of them)
- Game progression/Experience
- Difficulty/AI
- Loot/Items
- Crafting system

You won't be in the game for long until you start to see some of the bugs that were fairly abundant in my play through. From miniscule ones such as floating defilade/items (seems common to the Apex engine) to impactful ones as not being able to load my weapon, player getting stuck on terrain, or items randomly duplicating in your inventory (happened to a friend) to mention a few. They were also there to frustrate and pull you out of the immersion.

Experience system in itself is terribly designed. Playing MP the host will be the only one who obtains experience from completing missions which IMO is just ludicrous. Other players will still receive it for battles and discoveries but this was a huge deal breaker for me, as it essentially made us play each section twice myself and a friend switching off as the host. The perk system as well is terrible with very little impact on the game and feels very tacked on.

The difficulty is my largest issue over my play time. This game is way too easy even on higher difficulties, with virtually no threat whatsoever. Just looting you obtain a ridiculous amount of med kits which use is not limited in any way. You can just spam them at will and while you do have to equip to use them, this is nothing more than a minor inconvenience. I never even found the need to use the better quality ones as just spamming the lower tier kits were quite sufficient as hiding is made all the more easy by the unintelligent AI. Its hard to believe that these machines took over Sweden being as stupid as they are. There were fights where I literally just stood in the open shooting at them and received very little damage at all as they ran around me. You can pick them off at distance as they have trouble tracking you at length and sometimes found them having trouble detecting me just being almost at arms length. 

Both priors mentioned led to never really feeling threatened at all. I never died once so I can't even tell you what happens because you can easily even revive yourself with an adrenaline shot which just as with med kits, there is no limit to how many you can carry or how often you can use them. Eliminating all together the need to use hit-and-run tactics or traps with propane canisters/radios. Even the Tank-like enemies are of little threat, just more of an inconvenience as they are damage sponges.

Then there is the endless loot cycle of getting to a new location, search numerous backpacks, cars, containers to find absurd amounts of ammo, med packs, and seemingly useless crafting supplies. Also, less common you'll come across weapons or mods for those weapons which are annoying to keep finding a low tier silencer or scope over and over and over. When you finally find something interesting like a new weapon it is always the lowest tier which makes it pretty much useless as by then you probably have a gun that's a more reasonable quality. It's all just so tedious, like rummaging through a junk pile/drawer in your backyard or garage hoping to find something actually useful when you know the chances are slim. 

The crafting system is also horrible. 15 hours in and the best thing I can craft gives me a +1% bonus to defense against bullet damage, lol! Why am I collecting these resources? There are 4 or 5 things I can craft and they are all virtually worthless after 15 hours of collecting blueprints and resources, nuff said about this.   

In conclusion, it didn't take long for my rose-tinted glasses to wear off through my play time and they were replaced with a question that I asked myself; "why am I doing this?" There is no threat to my character, the story isn't good or bad really but the game doesn't make me care about it. The game seems to go out of its way to make me avoid the mechanics that are placed in it. The bugs continuously seem to discourage between the other frustrations of finding the same stuff in every container, having to replay boring missions over again with different hosts so that they get the XP, only to do it all over again when we discover a new location. But at least my guy looks dope and it’s the 80's.......  Na, I'd rather spend my time playing something else.

I bought this game several months ago as part of a sale. I had read the mixed reviews and was skeptical. The reviews seemed to be a perfect 50-50 split of either fantastic or trash. So I decided to play it for myself. 

I'll be honest the skill curve of this game is enormous. The robots are all Lethal and kill you with ease. While you as the player can barely put a dent in them. The beginning is very slow. You are going to die. A LOT. 

THIS GAME IS HARD. It is the DARK SOULS of the FPS GENRE.

But after completing a few of the story missions getting a Hunting Rifle, Shotgun, and an SMG. The game slowly but surely starts to become less and less frustrating and more fun.

 The Tutorial Island is massive, basically everything before you get to the bigger island is the tutorial area. This is where it either makes it or breaks it for most people. Most of the people calling the game trash are people who rushed through the story missions and didn't explore the tutorial island fully.

 They missed out on tons of experience, ammo, loot, and guns. Before charging headlong into dangerous enemies, as well as failing to learn the fundamentals of dealing with machines. Sure some figured out that the Fuel Cells on top of the runners are a critical component. And hitting it can dispatch them relatively easily. But most don't figure out that there are far more components in every machine and have either hit them by accident or sprayed 100's of rounds into a hunter to kill it. When you can kill them much more easily and quickly by targeting the components. Further more the difficulty ramps up ten fold once you cross that bridge into the main island. Hunters travel in packs of 3 or more, runners travel in packs of 3 to 15. Harvesters and Tanks are everywhere. And all they have are a trash tier pistol, a busted shotgun, and a rusty hunting rifle. And they get dunked on by everything.


But for the rest of us who explored the island, progressed our skill tree, took it slow at first, learned how to kill the robots efficiently by targeting components. Stockpiled hundreds of rounds, flares, fireworks, and med kits. Were far more ready to take on the mainland. 

THE TAKE AWAY: This game is amazing, It's intense, fast paced and I can play it for hours and feel sad that its time to sleep.
Don't treat this game the same as other looter shooters like borderlands. Treat it like generation zero. Explore everything, loot everything, kill everything, die over and over again. Get zerg rushed by that random hunter patrol that heard your gunshots from a kilometer away and most importantly have fun doing it.

Pros:
Fast paced combat
Hours of non-stop intense gameplay

Short review: The Game is still pretty poor as of Early-2022. Only buy it if you have friends, people you want to torture, or have cash to burn.

Longer Review:
Generation Zero is a game I return to on a yearly basis to see if it improved, but ultimately it's like that friend still couch-surfing with grandiose dreams. It's absolutely disappointing alone, but can be somewhat passable in a group of friends. Either way, Exploration and Combat both suck in equal measures, at times both can be involving and enjoyable but most of the time they're the games biggest traversal hindrance. Secondly, Skills add to that hindrance with abject baffling design choices where entire trees of skills are useless and there's no way to "Try Before you Invest" to see if they work out good in the long term. Finally, the drive to loot and gain power is ultimately dashed by nothing to progress towards.

Exploration is a pleasant aspect of the game, with the environments being interesting at least initially while the areas are close together. However, once the world opens up a bit getting to a point of interest is the biggest chore as you dodge patrols of dodgy AI programming and poor stealth mechanics. Sometimes the Robots are everywhere, roadblocking your way to a new juicy objective or area and that can get involving with ditching patrols and scurrying around in the underbrush like a field mouse. At other times, the games AI just bugs out and spots you from a mile away with pinpoint accuracy and sends a group of heavily armed robotic ass hats on your position to "f- that guy in particular".

At this point, Combat rears its bug-ugly head, which I must say is the most enjoyable part of the experience when not indoors. The guns do have that punch and they feel good from a gameplay standpoint, but ultimately just do what they say on the tin. Damage received from enemies is pretty easily healed through easily, even gas attacks, and combat only gets really frantic when there's no cover about. However, when there is cover via a building the combat just becomes a cake walk since bots can't enter structures and can be picked off one by one from the windows. Basically, the robots are sponges for you to waste your scant resources on, gain experience, and ultimately level up from.

Speaking of the Skills, most don't matter at all and you only get 31 of them without a respec or other option to try them to see if they're worth a damn. This is possibly the most player hostile system in the game at present and needs a dire tuning or rework. The "Support" Tree is a hard waste of points and only serves to waste your time with things like "Throw Distance/Accuracy" and "Marking Enemies" for limited benefit in both team and solo play. While the "Combat" and "Survival" trees are pretty solid choices no matter what you get up to with serious quality of life skills like faster Aim Down Sights and Recoil Control in "Combat" or the Carry Weight and Stealth Perks in "Survival". As for "Tech" it's an odd one as it doesn't provide a core benefit in most gameplay, outside of a select few perks (i.e. Lock picking and Component Damage) and while hacking might sound cool at first it has a Chance to work and that's if the AI doesn't bug out doing nothing. Specializations are also dubious investments with only two or three worth a damn, the rest are absolute dogwater choices and are a waste of precious points.

Finally, Loot the drive of any game, what the point of exploration and combat if there's nothing to strive for, right?. Well, GZ has none of that as there's really nothing of note to scavenge off the bots, except ammo. All the schematics are laying out in the open for players to find and pick-up, which amounts to mostly piss improvements to your overall survivability when crafted (A whole +1%, YAY!). Speaking of which, The game has a crafting system but doesn't utilize it, there's no improvised weaponry or equipment that you can craft from the parts of the fallen bots. Ammo and Med-kits are the sole things you'll be crafting, but you'll be drowning in them constantly along with the lack of actual swimming. This aspect alone is possibly the biggest let down in Generation Zero for me, it could of been a core element to progression and character development but ultimately does nothing.

Overall, the game is pretty flawed, but there could be something here if the Devs were given the time and effort to improve the base game. I hear the DLCs have some merit and improve the game, but spending money on something that should of been there from the get-go isn't a wise investment. Maybe next year...
